summary: Hundreds of women have sued Uber alleging it has not done enough to prevent sexual assaults by drivers, and a judicial panel has consolidated more than 80 cases in federal court. Survivors and their attorneys argue Uber's app-based safety features are inadequate and demand in-vehicle cameras, fingerprint background checks, driver training and better complaint systems. Uber's own safety reports show a lower assault rate but no improvement in the rape rate, and the company says it cannot comment on pending litigation.
one_line: More than 80 Uber sexual assault lawsuits are consolidated in federal court as survivors demand in-car cameras, fingerprint checks and stronger safety measures.
key_facts: A panel of judges ruled that more than 80 sexual assault cases against Uber can be consolidated into federal court.
The lawsuits claim Uber has known about sexual assaults by drivers since 2014.

Uber introduced a 911 button and location sharing with a friend in 2018, a feature to record audio during trips in 2021, and in 2022 a pilot with live help from an ADT safety agent plus PIN verification.
Rachel Abrams, a partner at Peiffer Wolf Carr Kane Conway & Wise, filed the petition to consolidate the cases and says mandatory in-vehicle cameras are "essential for safety."
Abrams says she has interviewed upward of 5,000 survivors and has seen no difference in the number of attacks before or after Uber's in-app features.
Abrams believes Uber is slow to adopt cameras not because of cost but because many drivers don't want them and Uber would lose drivers.
Uber uses third-party firms Checkr and Appriss for background checks, which the lawsuit calls "fast and shallow"; plaintiffs want fingerprinting against FBI databases.
Uber and Lyft say smudged fingerprints can give inaccurate results and arrest records can have discriminatory effects on minority communities.
Uber claims the reported sexual assault rate fell 38% between its first (2017-2018) and second (2019-2020) safety reports.
Total sexual assault reports across five categories fell from 5,981 to 3,824, while trips dropped from 1.4 billion in 2019 to 650 million in 2020.
The rape rate on the platform has remained the same since 2017, and Uber has not released safety data for 2021 and 2022.
Under Uber's terms of use, class action suits cannot be filed for sexual assault, so each case must be heard individually.
Judge Charles Breyer of the Northern District of California will preside over pretrial hearings, and Abrams expects proceedings to last one to two years.
Uber argues it did not owe plaintiffs a duty to protect against criminal conduct.
